Judaism. Judaism is an ancient, monotheistic Abrahamic religion, representing the collective religious, cultural, and legal tradition of the Jewish people across more than three millennia. Traced to the patriarch Abraham and crystallized through the covenant with Moses at Mount Sinai, it is the oldest surviving monotheistic faith tradition. The religion centers on the Torah, the sacred law, and emphasizes study, ethical conduct, and adherence to divine commandments called mitzvot as the path to holiness. Judaism has evolved from temple-based sacrificial worship to rabbinic interpretation and modern denominational expression, yet maintains unbroken continuity with its ancient sources. Its influence on Christianity and Islam, and its emphasis on textual learning and ethical reasoning, makes it foundational to Western and Middle Eastern civilization.

Judaism is the oldest of the three major Abrahamic religions, tracing lineage to patriarch Abraham, with whom God established the founding covenant. The Torah, also called the Pentateuch, comprises the first five books of the Hebrew Bible and is believed to have been revealed by God to Moses at Mount Sinai. Judaism holds the Tanakh, the Hebrew Bible, as scripture. The Talmud is the vast rabbinical text that interprets and applies Torah law to all circumstances. The central prayer is the Shema Yisrael: "Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one." It is the foundational declaration of absolute monotheism.

Judaism transitioned from a temple-based sacrificial cult with the Temple in Jerusalem as its center to a text- and rabbinic-focused tradition after Rome destroyed the Second Temple in seventy CE. Diaspora Judaism developed portable, community-centered practices centered on the synagogue and Torah study rather than temple sacrifice.

Modern Judaism encompasses Orthodox Judaism, which views Torah as immutable divine law; Conservative Judaism, which sees law as historically evolving but binding; and Reform Judaism, which emphasizes ethics and personal autonomy. Central practices include keeping Shabbat, the Sabbath; observing the six hundred thirteen mitzvot; following dietary laws called kashrut; and celebrating major holidays like Passover and Yom Kippur.

Judaism's resilience and adaptability—surviving exile, persecution, and diaspora across continents—is central to both its internal theology and its historical significance. Rabbinic Judaism, forged after the Temple's destruction, invented the structures of the synagogue, prayer, and textual study that allowed the tradition to survive without a physical center. This model profoundly influenced Christianity and Islam. The emphasis on Talmudic debate itself became spiritually central: argumentation and interpretation are acts of piety, not mere scholarship. In culture broadly, Judaism appears as the fountainhead of ethical monotheism, the source of the Decalogue and Prophetic tradition, and through its influence on Christianity and Islam, as a shaping force in world history.
